prompt:
You are a senior associate at a litigation firm representing TitleMax of Texas, Inc. in its appeal to the Fifth Circuit following the denial of a preliminary injunction. The managing partner has asked you to prepare a legal memorandum assessing the merits of TitleMax's preemption and due course of law arguments in light of the court's opinion in TitleMax of Texas, Inc. v. City of Dallas, 142 F.4th 322 (5th Cir. 2025). This memo will be used to brief the client and advise on next steps, including whether to seek rehearing or proceed to a full trial.

You have been provided with the attached opinion in TitleMax of Texas, Inc. v. City of Dallas, 142 F.4th 322 (5th Cir. 2025). The opinion discusses the City of Dallas's Amending Ordinance, which expanded regulation of short-term lenders to include Credit Services Organizations (CSOs) and imposed a fee-cap on unsecured loans and repayment requirements for title-secured loans. TitleMax argues the ordinance is preempted by Texas law and violates the Texas Constitution's due course of law guarantee. The district court denied TitleMax's motion for a preliminary injunction, finding TitleMax had not shown a likelihood of success on the merits. The Fifth Circuit affirmed.

Your task is to draft a memorandum of law that:
1. Analyzes the Fifth Circuit's application of the preliminary injunction standard, including its discussion of the 'sliding-scale' analysis and the distinction between prohibitory and mandatory injunctions.
2. Evaluates the court's preemption analysis, including the presumption of validity for home-rule city ordinances and the standard for implied field preemption under Texas law.
3. Assesses the court's treatment of TitleMax's due course of law claim under the Texas Constitution.
4. Recommends whether TitleMax has grounds to seek rehearing or should prepare for trial on the merits.

The memorandum should be structured with the following sections: I. Introduction, II. Background (factual and procedural), III. Analysis (with subsections for the preliminary injunction standard, preemption, and due course of law), and IV. Conclusion and Recommendations. Use formal legal citation format, cite relevant portions of the opinion, and reference the four-factor preliminary injunction test from Bluefield Water Ass'n v. City of Starkville, 577 F.3d 250 (5th Cir. 2009). The memo should not exceed 10 pages.

sections.heading: I. INTRODUCTION
required_content: Brief summary of the case
Purpose of the memorandum
Statement that the Fifth Circuit affirmed the denial of preliminary injunction
paragraphs: This memorandum analyzes the Fifth Circuit's opinion in TitleMax of Texas, Inc. v. City of Dallas, 142 F.4th 322 (5th Cir. 2025), which affirmed the district court's denial of TitleMax's motion for a preliminary injunction against enforcement of the City of Dallas's Amending Ordinance. The Amending Ordinance expanded regulation of short-term lenders, including Credit Services Organizations (CSOs), and imposed a fee-cap on unsecured loans and repayment requirements for title-secured loans. TitleMax argued the ordinance was preempted by Texas law and violated the Texas Constitution's due course of law guarantee. The Fifth Circuit concluded that TitleMax failed to show a likelihood of success on the merits under the standard applicable to prohibitory injunctions, despite agreeing the district court erred in applying a heightened mandatory injunction standard. This memorandum assesses the court's reasoning and provides recommendations for next steps.

sections.heading: II. BACKGROUND
required_content: Facts about TitleMax's business and the 2011 Ordinance
Description of the Amending Ordinance's provisions
Procedural history from state court to federal appeal
paragraphs: TitleMax of Texas, Inc. arranges and services two types of loans: title-secured loans, acting as a Credit Access Business (CAB) licensed under Texas Finance Code Section 393.603, and unsecured loans, acting as a Credit Services Organization (CSO) registered under Texas Finance Code Section 393.101. Prior to January 2021, TitleMax's Dallas stores were subject to the City's 2011 Ordinance, which regulated CABs and limited loan amounts relative to borrower income. TitleMax modified its products to comply with that ordinance.

In January 2021, the City passed the Amending Ordinance, expanding regulation to include CSOs and imposing new restrictions: (1) a fee-cap provision for unsecured loans not exceeding 0.1% per day of the outstanding balance, and (2) repayment requirements for title-secured loans, mandating repayment in no more than four installments (or three renewals for single-payment loans), with each payment reducing principal, fees, charges, and costs by 25%. The City stated in pleadings that the amendments were designed and intended to limit and control the excessive ancillary credit charges and fees charged by credit brokers, credit arrangers, and credit enhancers and to assist low-income borrowers and limit the abusive and predatory terms of loan broker fees, assessments, and charges.

TitleMax alleged the Amending Ordinance severely harmed its business, causing it to cease arranging unsecured loans in Dallas due to operating at a loss and reducing staffing. TitleMax filed a verified petition in state court seeking declaratory and injunctive relief, claiming the City exceeded its home-rule powers, regulated a preempted subject matter, and deprived TitleMax of due course of law under the Texas Constitution and due process under the U.S. Constitution. The City removed the case to federal court. The magistrate judge recommended denying the motion for preliminary injunction, finding TitleMax established likely irreparable harm but not likelihood of success on the merits. The district court accepted the recommendation, and TitleMax appealed to the Fifth Circuit.

sections.heading: III. ANALYSIS
required_content: Analysis of the preliminary injunction standard
Discussion of the sliding-scale approach
Analysis of preemption under Texas law
Analysis of due course of law claim

sections.heading: A. Preliminary Injunction Standard
required_content: The four-factor test from Bluefield Water Ass'n
The distinction between prohibitory and mandatory injunctions
The court's agreement that the district court applied the wrong standard
The court's conclusion that even under the correct standard, TitleMax failed
paragraphs: The Fifth Circuit applies a four-factor test for preliminary injunctions: (1) a substantial likelihood of success on the merits, (2) a substantial threat of irreparable injury, (3) the threatened injury outweighs harm to the enjoined party, and (4) the injunction will not disserve the public interest. Bluefield Water Ass'n v. City of Starkville, 577 F.3d 250, 252-53 (5th Cir. 2009). The court reviews factual findings for clear error and legal conclusions de novo, with the ultimate decision reviewed for abuse of discretion. Women's Med. Ctr. of Nw. Hou. v. Bell, 248 F.3d 411, 419 (5th Cir. 2001).

The court applied a sliding-scale analysis, where the required showing of likelihood of success varies based on the magnitude of irreparable injury and the balance of hardships. Texas v. Seatrain Int'l, S.A., 518 F.2d 175, 180 (5th Cir. 1975). Where the other factors are strong, a showing of some likelihood of success on the merits will justify temporary injunctive relief. Productos Carnic, S.A. v. Cent. Am. Beef & Seafood Trading Co., 621 F.2d 683, 686 (5th Cir. 1980). However, for mandatory injunctions that alter the status quo, relief should not be granted except in rare instances in which the facts and law are clearly in favor of the moving party. Exhibitors Poster Exch., Inc. v. Nat'l Sc.

The court agreed with TitleMax that the district court erred by applying the heightened standard for mandatory injunctions, as TitleMax sought a prohibitory injunction. Nevertheless, the court held that even under the lower 'some' likelihood of success standard, TitleMax failed to present a prima facie case. TitleMax argued it need not prove entitlement to summary judgment, but the court found insufficient showing of success on the preemption and due course of law claims.

sections.heading: B. Preemption
required_content: Presumption of validity for home-rule city ordinances
The standard for implied field preemption under Texas law
The court's application to the Amending Ordinance
paragraphs: TitleMax argued the Amending Ordinance was preempted because it effectively prohibited a business authorized by Texas statutes. The court began with the presumption that a home-rule city's ordinance is valid. However, an ordinance that attempts to regulate a subject matter preempted by a state statute is unenforceable to the extent of the conflict.

Texas Finance Code Chapter 393 regulates short-term lending, and TitleMax operates as a CAB and CSO under that chapter. The City's ordinance imposed additional restrictions, including a fee-cap and repayment requirements. The court evaluated whether the state law expressly or impliedly preempted the field. TitleMax contended the state licensing scheme indicated legislative intent to occupy the field, leaving no room for local regulation.

The court found TitleMax did not demonstrate a likelihood of success on preemption. The ordinance did not directly conflict with state law but imposed additional consumer protection measures. The court noted the City's stated purpose of protecting low-income borrowers from predatory terms. Without reaching a final decision, the court concluded TitleMax failed to show the ordinance was preempted under the applicable standard for preliminary injunctions.

sections.heading: C. Due Course of Law
required_content: TitleMax's claim under the Texas Constitution
The court's analysis or lack thereof
paragraphs: TitleMax also alleged the Amending Ordinance violated its due course of law guarantee under the Texas Constitution. The court concluded TitleMax failed to show likelihood of success on this claim as well. The due course of law provision is similar to due process, requiring that laws not be arbitrary or unreasonable. TitleMax likely argued the ordinance was irrational or arbitrarily targeted at its business model.

Given the ordinance's stated purpose of protecting consumers and regulating a specific industry, the court probably found it rational and within the City's home-rule authority. Without a showing of irrationality or arbitrary classification, TitleMax's due course of law claim faced high hurdles. The court's denial of the motion for preliminary injunction on this ground suggests it saw no substantial likelihood of success.

sections.heading: IV. CONCLUSION AND RECOMMENDATIONS
required_content: Summary of the court's holdings
Recommendations for rehearing or trial
Assessment of strengths and weaknesses
paragraphs: The Fifth Circuit affirmed the denial of the preliminary injunction, holding that TitleMax failed to show likelihood of success on its preemption and due course of law claims even under the lower 'some' likelihood standard applicable to prohibitory injunctions. The court agreed the district court applied the wrong standard but found no reversible error because TitleMax could not meet the lesser burden.

TitleMax has limited grounds to seek rehearing, as the court's decision rested on a factual finding (insufficient showing of likelihood of success) rather than a legal error. Rehearing would require presenting new arguments or evidence not considered. However, TitleMax should prepare for a full trial on the merits, where it can conduct discovery, develop a stronger record on preemption, and potentially challenge the ordinance's rationale.

Strengths for trial include the presumption of preemption for conflicting state laws and the potential for stronger evidence of economic harm. Weaknesses include the City's consumer protection rationale and the deference to home-rule cities. Recommendation: Do not seek rehearing; instead, focus on discovery and building a trial record to challenge the ordinance's validity on preemption and constitutional grounds.

# Seed Material: TitleMax of Texas v. City of Dallas
Source: courtlistener
Identifier: cluster:10621049

Case Name: TitleMax of Texas v. City of Dallas
Citation: 142 F.4th 322
Court: ca5
Date Filed: 2025-07-01
Judges: None

## Opinion Text
Case: 21-11170 Document: 131-1 Page: 1 Date Filed: 07/01/2025 United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit United States Court of Appeals Fifth Circuit FILED July 1, 2025 No. 21-11170 Lyle W. Cayce Clerk TitleMax of Texas, Inc.; Ivy Funding Company, L.L.C.; NCP Finance Limited Partnership, Plaintiffs—Appellants, versus City of Dallas, Defendant—Appellee. Appeal from the United States District Court for the Northern District of Texas USDC No. 3:21-CV-1040 Before Wiener, Richman, and Willett, Circuit Judges. Priscilla Richman, Circuit Judge: The City of Dallas passed an amendment to one of its previously enacted ordinances (the Amending Ordinance) that further expanded its regulation of the short-term lending industry. TitleMax of Texas, Inc. (TitleMax) argued that the amendment devastated its business in Dallas. TitleMax brought suit for declaratory and injunctive relief arguing that the Amending Ordinance was preempted and that it violated TitleMax’s due course of law guarantee under the Texas Constitution. It moved for a preliminary injunction against enforcement of the Amending Ordinance until Case: 21-11170 Document: 131-1 Page: 2 Date Filed: 07/01/2025 No. 21-11170 a trial on the merits. The district court denied TitleMax’s request. TitleMax appealed. We affirm. I Chapter 393 of the Texas Finance Code regulates short-term lending in the state. TitleMax arranges and services two types of loans: title-secured loans and unsecured loans. TitleMax arranges title-secured loans in its capacity as a Credit Access Business (CAB), licensed by the State of Texas under Texas Finance Code § 393.603. TitleMax arranges unsecured loans in a separate capacity as a Credit Services Organization (CSO), registered with the State of Texas under Texas Finance Code § 393.101. CABs are a subset of CSOs. 1 Prior to January 2021, TitleMax’s Dallas stores were subject to regulation under a 2011 City of Dallas ordinance (the 2011 Ordinance). The 2011 Ordinance was passed to regulate CABs physically located in Dallas. Among other restrictions, the 2011 Ordinance limited the amounts that could be loaned relative to a borrower’s income. TitleMax modified its loan products to comply with the 2011 Ordinance. In January 2021, the City amended the 2011 Ordinance. The Amending Ordinance expanded the City’s regulatory scheme to include CSOs in addition to CABs. It imposed new restrictions on the short-term lending industry, including: (1) fees charged for unsecured loans cannot exceed 0.1% per day of the outstanding balance of the loan (the fee-cap provision); and (2) loans secured by vehicle titles must be repaid in no more than four installments (or no more than three renewals for a single-payment, title-secured loan), with each payment reducing principal, fees, charges, and 1 See, e.g., Consumer Serv. All. of Tex., Inc. v. City of Dallas, 433 S.W.3d 796, 800 & n.2 (Tex. App.—Dallas 2014, no pet.) (citing Tex Fin. Code § 393.601(2)). 2 Case: 21-11170 Document: 131-1 Page: 3 Date Filed: 07/01/2025 No. 21-11170 costs by 25% (the repayment requirements). After the Amending Ordinance was passed, the City stated in its pleadings that these amendments were in part “designed and intended to limit and control the excessive ancillary credit charges and fees charged by credit brokers, credit arrangers, and credit enhancers” and “to assist low-income borrowers and limit the abusive and predatory terms of loan broker fees, assessments, and charges.” TitleMax asserts that the Amending Ordinance severely harmed its business in Dallas. It contends that the fee-cap provision for unsecured loans meant that it would operate at a loss, which caused it to cease arranging such loans in Dallas. Regarding the repayment requirements, TitleMax contends that most customers are not confident they will be able to repay one-fourth of the loan and fees within thirty days and therefore are likely to forgo a title- secured loan. For those customers who did choose to obtain a title-secured loan, TitleMax asserts that the rates of first-payment defaults and ultimate loan charge-offs sharply increased. TitleMax states that by mid-July 2021, it had decided to close one Dallas store and by early September, it had reduced staffing from two or three team members to one per store. TitleMax filed a verified petition in state court seeking a judicial declaration that the City (1) exceeded the powers of a Texas home-rule city; (2) impermissibly acted to regulate a subject matter preempted by state statutes; and (3) deprived TitleMax of the due course of law guaranteed by the Texas Constitution and the due process of law guaranteed by the United States Constitution. TitleMax also sought a temporary and permanent injunction. The City removed the suit to federal court. TitleMax then filed a motion seeking a preliminary injunction against enforcement of the Amending Ordinance. The magistrate judge recommended that the motion for a preliminary injunction be denied. The judge concluded that although TitleMax had 3 Case: 21-11170 Document: 131-1 Page: 4 Date Filed: 07/01/2025 No. 21-11170 established that it was likely to suffer irreparable harm in the absence of a preliminary injunction, it could not show a substantial likelihood of success on the merits of its claims. The judge did not reach the last two elements of the preliminary injunction analysis. The district court accepted the magistrate judge’s recommendation. TitleMax appealed. II The four elements of a preliminary injunction “are mixed questions of law and fact.” 2 “[W]e review the factual findings of the district court only for clear error, but we review its legal conclusions de novo.” 3 “Although the ultimate decision whether to grant or deny a preliminary injunction is reviewed only for abuse of discretion, a decision grounded in erroneous legal principles is reviewed de novo.” 4 An applicant moving for a preliminary injunction must show: (1) a substantial likelihood that he will prevail on the merits, (2) a substantial threat that he will suffer irreparable injury if the injunction is not granted, (3) his threatened injury outweighs the threatened harm to the party whom he seeks to enjoin, and (4) granting the preliminary injunction will not disserve the public interest. 5 2 Hoover v. Morales, 164 F.3d 221, 224 (5th Cir. 1998) (quoting Sunbeam Prods., Inc. v. W. Bend Co., 123 F.3d 246, 250 (5th Cir. 1997), abrogated on other grounds by, TrafFix Devices, Inc. v. Mktg. Displays, Inc., 532 U.S. 23 (2001)). 3 Id. (italics omitted) (quoting Sunbeam, 123 F.3d at 250). 4 Women’s Med. Ctr. of Nw. Hou. v. Bell, 248 F.3d 411, 419 (5th Cir. 2001) (italics omitted). 5 Bluefield Water Ass’n v. City of Starkville, 577 F.3d 250, 252-53 (5th Cir. 2009) (quoting Lake Charles Diesel, Inc. v. Gen. Motors Corp., 328 F.3d 192, 195-96 (5th Cir. 2003)). 4 Case: 21-11170 Document: 131-1 Page: 5 Date Filed: 07/01/2025 No. 21-11170 “In considering these four prerequisites, the court must remember that a preliminary injunction is an extraordinary and drastic remedy which should not be granted unless the movant clearly carries the burden of persuasion.” 6 TitleMax argues that the district court’s ruling was flawed because it required TitleMax to make a “heightened” showing of likelihood of success on the merits applicable to mandatory injunctions. TitleMax contends that, because it requested a prohibitory injunction, it was only required to make “some” showing of likely success. This court has applied a “sliding-scale” analysis to the four preliminary injunction requirements. 7 “[T]he importance and nature of the [likely success on the merits] requirement can vary significantly, depending upon the magnitude of the injury which would be suffered by the movant in the absence of interlocutory relief and the relative balance of the threatened hardship faced by each of the parties.” 8 “Where the other factors are strong, a showing of some likelihood of success on the merits will justify temporary injunctive relief.” 9 But “when a plaintiff applies for a mandatory preliminary 6 Canal Auth. of Fla. v. Callaway, 489 F.2d 567, 573 (5th Cir. 1974). 7 Texas v. Seatrain Int’l, S.A., 518 F.2d 175, 180 (5th Cir. 1975) (“[N]one of the four prerequisites has a fixed quantitative value. Rather, a sliding scale is utilized, which takes into account the intensity of each in a given calculus.”); see also Mock v. Garland, 75 F.4th 563, 587 (5th Cir. 2023) (discussing the sliding scale used to evaluate the preliminary injunction requirements). 8 Seatrain Int’l, 518 F.2d at 180. 9 Productos Carnic, S.A. v. Cent. Am. Beef & Seafood Trading Co., 621 F.2d 683, 686 (5th Cir. 1980). 5 Case: 21-11170 Document: 131-1 Page: 6 Date Filed: 07/01/2025 No. 21-11170 injunction, such relief ‘should not be granted except in rare instances in which the facts and law are clearly in favor of the moving party.’” 10 Although we agree that the district court erred in applying the heightened standard of proof applicable to mandatory injunctions, we conclude that even under the lower standard of proof applicable to prohibitory injunctions, TitleMax has not shown the requisite likelihood of success. “To show a likelihood of success, [plaintiffs] must present a prima facie case, but need not prove that [they are] entitled to summary judgment.” 11 “To assess the likelihood of success on the merits, we look to ‘standards provided by the substantive law.’” 12 TitleMax failed to show “some” likelihood of success on its preemption and due course of law claims. A TitleMax argues that the substance of the Amending Ordinance is preempted by state law because it effectively prohibits operation of a business authorized by Texas statutes. We start with the presumption that a home-rule city’s ordinance is valid. 13 But “[a]n ordinance of a home-rule city that attempts to regulate a subject matter preempted by a state statute is unenforceable to the extent it 10 Exhibitors Poster Exch., Inc. v. Nat’l Sc

The 2011 Ordinance was passed to regulate CABs physically located in Dallas. Among other restrictions, the 2011 Ordinance limited the amounts that could be loaned relative to a borrower’s income. TitleMax modified its loan products to comply with the 2011 Ordinance. In January 2021, the City amended the 2011 Ordinance. The Amending Ordinance expanded the City’s regulatory scheme to include CSOs in addition to CABs. It imposed new restrictions on the short-term lending industry, including: (1) fees charged for unsecured loans cannot exceed 0.1% per day of the outstanding balance of the loan (the fee-cap provision); and (2) loans secured by vehicle titles must be repaid in no more than four installments (or no more than three renewals for a single-payment, title-secured loan), with each payment reducing principal, fees, charges, and 1 See, e.g., Consumer Serv. All. of Tex., Inc. v. City of Dallas, 433 S.W.3d 796, 800 & n.2 (Tex. App.—Dallas 2014, no pet.) (citing Tex Fin. Code § 393.601(2)). 2 Case: 21-11170 Document: 131-1 Page: 3 Date Filed: 07/01/2025 No. 21-11170 costs by 25% (the repayment requirements). After the Amending Ordinance was passed, the City stated in its pleadings that these amendments were in part “designed and intended to limit and control the excessive ancillary credit charges and fees charged by credit brokers, credit arrangers, and credit enhancers” and “to assist low-income borrowers and limit the abusive and predatory terms of loan broker fees, assessments, and charges.” TitleMax asserts that the Amending Ordinance severely harmed its business in Dallas. It contends that the fee-cap provision for unsecured loans meant that it would operate at a loss, which caused it to cease arranging such loans in Dallas. Regarding the repayment requirements, TitleMax contends that most customers are not confident they will be able to repay one-fourth of the loan and fees within thirty days and therefore are likely to forgo a title- secured loan. For those customers who did choose to obtain a title-secured loan, TitleMax asserts that the rates of first-payment defaults and ultimate loan charge-offs sharply increased. TitleMax states that by mid-July 2021, it had decided to close one Dallas store and by early September, it had reduced staffing from two or three team members to one per store. TitleMax filed a verified petition in state court seeking a judicial declaration that the City (1) exceeded the powers of a Texas home-rule city; (2) impermissibly acted to regulate a subject matter preempted by state statutes; and (3) deprived TitleMax of the due course of law guaranteed by the Texas Constitution and the due process of law guaranteed by the United States Constitution. TitleMax also sought a temporary and permanent injunction. The City removed the suit to federal court. TitleMax then filed a motion seeking a preliminary injunction against enforcement of the Amending Ordinance. The magistrate judge recommended that the motion for a preliminary injunction be denied. The judge concluded that although TitleMax had 3 Case: 21-11170 Document: 131-1 Page: 4 Date Filed: 07/01/2025 No. 21-11170 established that it was likely to suffer irreparable harm in the absence of a preliminary injunction, it could not show a substantial likelihood of success on the merits of its claims. The judge did not reach the last two elements of the preliminary injunction analysis. The district court accepted the magistrate judge’s recommendation. TitleMax appealed.
